# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is the most methodologically careful document in the series. It engages directly with each earlier claim and is honest about its limits. The core findings are credible:
- a per-hour gain that has declined but persists, under strict measures;
- the counter arm closed because service deteriorated;
- a Halden subset framed explicitly as survivors.

Three things need fixing or qualifying before the summary's wording can stand:
- the headline mixes two hours measures;
- an unplanned change in two control offices biases the decline estimate;
- the new log-based hours measure doesn't reconcile with the meeting data.

## Arithmetic checks

**Correct:**
- **Per-hour gains at 24 months:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% (timesheets) and 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% (logs).
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, so hours fell 13.4%; 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Counter-arm cost:** 12% more staff giving 9% higher cost per contact is plausible if labour is about three-quarters of cost. That assumption should be stated.

**Inconsistent:**
- **The summary compares different measures.** "Fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" sets the 9-month *timesheet* figure against the 24-month *log* figure. On a like-for-like basis the decline is 12.5% to 9.8%, about a fifth. Section 5's "about a quarter" sits between the two readings (22% and 32%). The summary should use 12.5% → 9.8% and give 8.5% separately as the stricter measure.

## Strengths

- Log data are added to capture unclaimed work, which was the gap I flagged in the nine-month report.
- The mediation test was registered before 24-month outcomes were available.
- Waiting times are now reported against control offices (7.3 v 4.0 minutes), with a cost estimate. The county ending the counter arm is itself strong evidence.
- The authors report the control-office meeting audit even though it complicates their story.
- The Halden continuers are framed honestly as "survivors twice over."
- The rebuttals are well targeted:
  - **Meta-analysis:** the four long studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the confounding concern raised earlier.
  - **Halden re-analysis:** it gets credit where it was right.

## Main problems

**1. The control-office meeting audit contaminates the comparison.**
- Two of the seven control offices raised output per hour by about 4.1% after cutting meetings in month 15.
- That raises the control average by roughly 1.2 points (2/7 × 4.1) and narrows the treated–control gap by a similar amount.
- So part of the apparent fade from 12.5% to 9.8% may be control offices improving, not treated offices declining.
- Plausibly the audits were prompted by the published nine-month finding, which would be classic spillover between trial arms.
- **What to report:**
  - a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or truncating their data at month 15;
  - an explicit statement that the decline may be overstated.
- The same observation also gives independent, if weak, support for the meetings hypothesis, which the authors do note.

**2. The decline is described but not tested.**
- The confidence intervals overlap almost entirely: +6.9 to +18.4 at nine months and +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months.
- "Consistent with some fading" is fair. So is "consistent with no change."
- Monthly data exist, so a trajectory across months 9 to 24 with a test of the slope would be far more informative than two points. Two-point extrapolation is the same weakness the authors rightly criticise in the Halden re-analysis.

**3. The log measure and the meeting data don't reconcile.**
- Logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases." That would exclude recurring meetings.
- A rough accounting, using the nine-month baseline of 37.9 hours:

  | Item | Treated vs control change |
  |---|---|
  | Total hours (−12%) | about −4.5 h |
  | Meeting time (−3.5 h treated, −0.2 h control) | about −3.3 h |
  | Non-meeting hours | about −1.2 h, roughly −4% of ~30.5 h |
  | Output per FTE | −3.4% |
  | Implied output per non-meeting hour | about +0.6% |

- This creates two tensions:
  - **The log fall looks too large.** If logs measure case work, they should fall by about 4%, not 11%. Either logs include logged-in meeting time, or they measure something other than described.
  - **The accounting leaves little room for other pathways.** Almost the entire timesheet gain coincides with reallocating time away from meetings. That fits poorly with a 47% meeting share, an 18% fatigue share and 35% unexplained. One explanation would be that the meetings had real output value.
- The authors should state exactly what log time captures and reconcile these figures.
- If logs do exclude meetings, then meetings affecting output per *case-hour* implies a different mechanism. That would be less fragmented work, not simply time freed up, and it is a different claim from the nine-month report's "removing low-value time."

**4. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result.**
- **Not an independent replication.** The hypothesis was generated in these same seven treated offices. Registering before the 24-month data closes off analytic flexibility. It does not replicate the finding in new units. "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated, correlated observations from the same 14 clusters.
- **The mediator–outcome link is observational,** as the limitations note. Offices whose managers cut meetings may differ in other ways, such as management quality.
- **The intervals look narrow for 14 clusters** (28–66%). The paper should state how clustering was handled and whether a correction for few clusters was applied.
- **Baseline meeting data need explaining.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Pre-period figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours) now appear, presumably from calendars retrieved after the fact. The paper should say so.
- **"Supports" would be the accurate word.** The fatigue pathway's interval (2–34%) also only just excludes zero.

**5. A baseline for the log measure is missing.**
- A difference-in-differences on log hours needs pre-period log data. The measure was "added" at follow-up.
- If the system retains historical logs, the paper should say so. If it doesn't, the −11% isn't a true difference-in-differences.
- The headline per-hour estimate also now rests on a measure introduced after the interim results, with no 9-month comparator. That is legitimate, but it makes the trend harder to read.

**6. The Halden section has three issues.**
- **One reversion doesn't fit the summary's description.** The summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." The marketing agency cited client deadlines, which is discretionary work by the meta-analysis's coding. The finding is that one discretionary organisation also reverted, and the summary blurs that.
- **Only 14 of the 23 organisations responded.** The nine non-responders may differ, quite possibly including more that reverted.
- **The baseline hours figure needs checking.** It is 40.3, exactly the mean for the re-analysis's 27 time-tracking organisations, not the 17-organisation subset (40.4) or these 11. Confirm it refers to the same 11 organisations. It is also unclear whether all 11 have time tracking.

**7. Two earlier issues remain open.**
- **Sick days (−27%):** these are still counted per FTE per year, which falls mechanically under a four-day week. A rate per scheduled day is still needed.
- **Resignations:** these are still raw rates between arms, without a difference-in-differences or intervals.

## Disclosure

Okafor is an author of the original Halden pilot, and the Varden authors are adjudicating criticism of their own work. Nothing here looks improper, and the Halden section is notably self-critical. A brief note on authors' roles would still be appropriate given Section 5.

## Bottom line

**What this report supports:**
- In randomised, discretionary public-sector work, a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years, under record-based output and strict hours measures.
- Output per employee is slightly below control at −3.4%, with a confidence interval that includes zero.
- In coverage-bound work, the scheme was abandoned because service and cost deteriorated.

**What remains unsettled:**
- **Whether the gain is still declining.** This needs a trajectory analysis and correction for the control-office contamination.
- **How much of the gain comes from meetings rather than hours.** The meeting-audit offices hint that reorganisation without shorter hours captures some of it. As the authors say, no arm tested that directly.

**Across all five documents:**
- The extreme claims have both failed: "sector-general" on one side, "entirely an artifact" on the other.
- The evidence converges on a modest per-hour gain in discretionary work, possibly fading slowly.
- That gain is substantially linked to cutting meetings, a change that might not require reduced hours.
- Coverage-bound work shows a clear loss.

The decisive next study would add an arm that reorganises work without reducing hours.
